subtype: Appeals to emotion, authority and logic [Interpreting]
passage: I was picking up my laptop charger when I saw Lalit stopped at a stall in the college corridor. A senior was handing out leaflets for a coaching course, saying, "Thousands of students like you have already changed their lives. Only three seats left today." Lalit took the leaflet and read it slowly. The senior kept talking. "Ask any topper. Don't be the one who regrets it." I saw Lalit hesitate with his phone in his hand. Then he asked, "Can I see last year's results, all of them, not only the top five? And can I think it over till Monday?" The senior's smile stiffened a little. I don't know what Lalit decided, and I don't know if the seats were real. But he walked away with the leaflet, not a receipt.

qa.q: How many seats did the senior say were left?
qa.a: The senior said only three seats were left today.

qa.q: What might Lalit have been feeling when he hesitated with his phone, and what else could it mean?
qa.a: He was likely tempted and a little worried about missing out, though he could also have been checking the price or texting a friend.

qa.q: What did Lalit do that a wise person might copy?
qa.a: He asked for all the results, not just the best ones, and asked for time until Monday instead of deciding under pressure.

qa.q: How might the senior see Lalit's questions?
qa.a: The senior may find them awkward if the offer depends on a quick yes, though they may simply be doing a job and mean no harm.

grounding: Lalit spots urgency and fear-based appeals in a sales pitch and weighs the evidence.

subtype: Appeals to emotion, authority and logic [Interpreting]
passage:
Week one. Rukmini's phone buzzed with a message from her cousin Aparna: "You'll break my heart if you don't lend me the money for the course. Everyone in the family already agreed." Rukmini felt guilty at once. She said she'd think about it.

Week two. She noticed the message had used love, pressure and the family's names, but no fees, dates or repayment plan. She asked, "What's the course, how long, and when could you pay back?" Aparna sent a long reply with all of it, plus a link to the class.

Week three. Rukmini lent part of it, in writing, after speaking with her father. She wasn't sure the emotional message had been manipulation. It had been a worried cousin asking, but the questions had made it clearer.

qa.q: What did Aparna's first message say she would do if Rukmini did not lend the money?
qa.a: She said Rukmini would break her heart.

qa.q: What did Rukmini feel when she first read the message, and what did she later notice about it?
qa.a: She felt guilty at once, and later noticed that it leaned on love and the family's names but gave no fees, dates or repayment plan.

qa.q: What worked well for Rukmini in handling the request?
qa.a: She asked for the details, put the lending in writing and spoke with her father, so she could help without acting only from guilt.

qa.q: What might Aparna have been feeling when she sent the first message?
qa.a: Aparna may have been anxious about missing the course and reached for emotional words because she felt short of money, without meaning to pressure.

grounding: Rukmini identifies emotional appeals in a personal request and weighs the evidence without assuming manipulation.

subtype: Appeals to emotion, authority and logic [Interpreting]
passage: Manjula, you asked me why I read every leaflet twice. Let your Raghav mama tell you. When I was twenty, a man came to our college with a "guaranteed rank" coaching course. He was very good. First he talked about our parents' sacrifices until half the room had tears in their eyes. Then he showed a photo of himself with a big officer: "Sir himself recommends us." Then he said, "Only ten seats left, and the offer ends tonight. You boys are clearly the smartest in this district." I wanted to sign right there. My friend Babloo nudged me. "Where are the results? Names? Numbers?" The man said, "Trust me." That was all. We didn't sign. Two months later, the course shut down. Emotion isn't always a trick, beti. But when it comes with hurry, fear and praise, and no proof, look twice.

qa.q: What did the man say about how many seats were left?
qa.a: Only ten seats left, and the offer ends tonight.

qa.q: How did young Raghav feel during the salesman's talk?
qa.a: He was moved and eager, wanting to sign right there, after the talk about parents' sacrifices and the flattery.

qa.q: What turning point in the story stopped Raghav from signing?
qa.a: His friend Babloo asked for results, names and numbers, and the man could only say "Trust me."

qa.q: How did the room react to the part about parents' sacrifices?
qa.a: Half the room had tears in their eyes, showing how strongly the emotional appeal worked on them.

grounding: Shows a young adult learning to spot emotional, authority and flattery appeals with urgency, and to ask for evidence.

subtype: Appeals to emotion, authority and logic [Interpreting]
passage: It was the night before Reena's own exam when Chinmay messaged her. "Reena, you're the only one who can save me. My assignment is due at nine tomorrow. Please write it? You're a genius, seriously. If I fail, my dad will kill me." Reena stared at the phone. Her chest tightened. She did like Chinmay, and she felt awful imagining him in trouble. But she noticed how the message was built: flattery, fear, a deadline in twelve hours. And her own exam was at ten. She typed slowly. "I'm sorry you're stressed. I can't write it for you, and I have my exam. But I can send you my notes on the topic and you can call me for fifteen minutes at seven." Chinmay replied, "Fine, thanks." At seven he did call, with questions. She answered, then went back to her own books.

qa.q: When was Chinmay's assignment due?
qa.a: At nine tomorrow.

qa.q: What was Reena feeling when she read Chinmay's message?
qa.a: She felt tense and torn, her chest tightening, because she cared about him and felt awful, but her own exam was the next day.

qa.q: What helped Reena respond wisely?
qa.a: She noticed the flattery, fear and deadline in the message, said no to writing it, and offered smaller help that fit her own time.

qa.q: How might Chinmay have felt when Reena said no?
qa.a: He may have felt disappointed, replying only "Fine, thanks", but he still called and got useful help.

grounding: Shows a young adult noticing flattery, fear and urgency in a personal request and weighing it before acting.

subtype: Appeals to emotion, authority and logic [Interpreting]
passage: At the Mumbai mall, two stalls stood side by side. At the first, a volunteer from an animal shelter showed Anjali and Tejas photos of rescued dogs. "We feed eighty dogs a day. Here's our last year's report and the vet's details. Donate if you want; no pressure." Anjali's eyes softened. At the second stall, a man in a crisp shirt stopped them with a loud voice. "Water in your building is poisoning your kids. Scientists agree. Our filter, today only, half price. Families like yours deserve the best." Tejas's face went pale. "Poison? Should we call Mummy?" Anjali pulled him aside. "Wait. The dog people gave a report. This man gave 'scientists agree' and 'today only'. No name. No test." Tejas breathed out. They took the shelter's leaflet and walked past the filter stall. At home, they looked up the building's last water test. It was fine.

qa.q: How many dogs does the shelter say it feeds a day?
qa.a: Eighty dogs a day.

qa.q: What was Anjali feeling at the shelter stall?
qa.a: Her eyes softened, suggesting she felt moved and warm toward the rescued dogs, without feeling pushed.

qa.q: How did Anjali tell the two appeals apart?
qa.a: The shelter's emotional appeal came with a report and vet details and no pressure, while the filter pitch used fear, vague authority, flattery and urgency without proof.

qa.q: What would change if Tejas had acted on his fear at the stall?
qa.a: He might have rushed into buying the filter today only, without checking the building's water test, which turned out to be fine.

grounding: Shows a young adult weighing appeals to emotion and authority, trusting evidence and scrutinising urgency, fear and flattery.

subtype: Appeals to emotion, authority and logic [Interpreting]
passage:
At the career fair, a man in a blazer had just finished his pitch, and Eshaan was already reaching for the form.
"Farida, did you hear him? Only ten seats left, and a famous professor designed the course. I should sign up now."
"Wait. Let's split what he actually said. Ten seats, decide today: that's urgency."
"Okay, but the professor?"
"That's authority. Could be real. Did he say which professor, or what the course covers?"
"...No. He said I look like someone who'll go far."
"And that's flattery. Nice, but it isn't evidence."
"So it's all a trick?"
"Not all. The bit about past students' placements was an argument, and he had a printed list. That's the part to check. And feeling excited isn't wrong. I felt it too."
"So what do I do?"
"Take the brochure, ask for the list, look up the professor tonight. If the seats vanish by tomorrow, they vanish."
Eshaan slowly put the pen down. "My heart's racing and nothing's even happened."

qa.q: How many seats did the man say were left?
qa.a: Ten.

qa.q: Why was Farida wary of the pitch?
qa.a: Farida felt cautious and suspicious of the urgency and flattery, while honestly admitting to feeling excited too.

qa.q: What does Farida suggest instead of signing on the spot?
qa.a: Take the brochure, ask for the placement list, look up the professor that night, and accept that seats may vanish.

qa.q: What was the pitch like for Eshaan?
qa.a: It left Eshaan excited and rushed, heart racing, ready to sign before knowing what the course covered.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult picking out appeals to urgency, authority, flattery and evidence in a sales pitch and weighing the evidence before acting.
